steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper Entropy-MCMC, a sampler for Bayesian neural networks that targets flat basins. Motivate why posterior inference should prioritize flat modes, explain why doing so efficiently is hard, introduce our method at a high level, and list the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Posterior estimation for BNNs is hard; flat vs sharp modes and generalization
- Existing Bayesian methods ignore flatness; why prioritize flat modes
- Efficiency challenge of biasing toward flat basins
- Our method: auxiliary guiding variable, theory and experiments
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Background
  - BNN effectiveness depends on posterior estimation quality
  - full posterior: high-dimensional, highly multi-modal -> very hard (cite x2)
  - modes differ in generalization: flat = better accuracy and robustness, sharp = high generalization error (cite x3)
  - geometry-generalization link -> optimization work: theory (cite x4), new algorithms (cite x4)
- Gap
  - most Bayesian methods unaware of flatness in posterior inference (cite x4)
  - energy-oriented; can't tell flat from sharp modes with same energy
  - hurts generalization, esp. when full posterior too costly
  - we argue: prioritize flat modes in BNN posterior inference
    - better generalization (prev. works, cite x3)
    - Bayesian marginalization view: each config in flat basin has big volume, contributes to predictive distribution (cite)
  - flatness-aware methods use one solution for whole basin (cite x2), ignore many good models in it
  - sampling from flat basins can improve over flatness-aware optimization (cite x2)
- Efficiency challenge
  - explicit bias to flat basins = big overhead even for point estimates
  - nested loops (cite x2), doubled gradient calculation (cite x2), min-max problems (cite)
  - must fix efficiency before practical for deep nets
- Our method
  - efficient sampler explicitly prioritizing flat basins in DNN energy landscape
  - auxiliary guiding variable \bm{\theta}_{a} in Markov chain pulls \bm{\theta} toward flat basins each step (Fig. 1a)
  - \bm{\theta}_{a} from smoothed posterior removing sharp modes via local entropy (cite) (Fig. 1b)
  - also = Gaussian convolution, common in diffusion models (cite x2)
  - simple joint distribution; overhead like SGLD (cite)
  - theory: converges faster than some flatness-aware methods (cite x2) in strongly convex setting
  - empirically finds flat basins efficiently on multiple tasks
- Contributions
  - Entropy-MCMC (EMCMC): auxiliary guiding variable + simple joint distribution
  - convergence proof; faster than several flatness-aware methods (strongly convex)
  - experiments: beats all baselines on classification, calibration, OOD detection; overhead comparable to SGLD
  - code at https://github.com/lblaoke/EMCMC

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
How well Bayesian neural networks work depends heavily on how good the estimate of the posterior distribution is. But it is extremely difficult to estimate the full posterior accurately because it is high-dimensional and highly multi-modal. Also, the many modes in the energy landscape usually have different generalization performance. Flat modes often have better accuracy and robustness, while sharp modes tend to have high generalization errors. This connection between the geometry of the energy landscape and generalization has led to many works in optimization, from theoretical understanding to new optimization algorithms.

However, most existing Bayesian methods do not pay attention to the flatness of the energy landscape when they do posterior inference. Their inference strategies are usually energy-oriented, so they cannot tell apart flat and sharp modes that have the same energy values. This can significantly hurt their generalization performance, especially in practice where it is too costly to capture the full posterior. Because of this, we argue that it is essential to prioritize capturing flat modes when doing posterior inference for Bayesian neural networks. This helps generalization, as previous works have justified. It also makes sense from a Bayesian marginalization point of view: in the flat basin, each model configuration takes up a substantial volume and contributes a lot to estimating the predictive distribution more precisely. Also, existing flatness-aware methods often use a single solution to represent the whole flat basin, and they ignore that the flat basin has many high-performing models in it. So Bayesian marginalization, by sampling from the flat basins, could potentially give significant improvements over flatness-aware optimization.

- Efficiency challenge
  - biasing to flat basins is costly even for point estimates: nested loops, doubled gradients, min-max problems
  - must be solved before practical for deep nets
- Our method
  - auxiliary guiding variable \bm{\theta}_{a} pulls \bm{\theta} toward flat basins each step (Fig. 1a)
  - sampled from smoothed posterior via local entropy (Fig. 1b); like Gaussian convolution in diffusion models
  - simple joint distribution; overhead like SGLD
  - faster convergence than some flatness-aware methods (strongly convex); finds flat basins on multiple tasks
- Contributions
  - EMCMC; convergence proof; experiments (classification, calibration, OOD detection); code at https://github.com/lblaoke/EMCMC

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
How well Bayesian neural networks work depends heavily on how good the estimate of the posterior distribution is. But it is extremely difficult to estimate the full posterior accurately because it is high-dimensional and highly multi-modal. Also, the many modes in the energy landscape usually have different generalization performance. Flat modes often have better accuracy and robustness, while sharp modes tend to have high generalization errors. This connection between the geometry of the energy landscape and generalization has led to many works in optimization, from theoretical understanding to new optimization algorithms.

However, most existing Bayesian methods do not pay attention to the flatness of the energy landscape when they do posterior inference. Their inference strategies are usually energy-oriented, so they cannot tell apart flat and sharp modes that have the same energy values. This can significantly hurt their generalization performance, especially in practice where it is too costly to capture the full posterior. Because of this, we argue that it is essential to prioritize capturing flat modes when doing posterior inference for Bayesian neural networks. This helps generalization, as previous works have justified. It also makes sense from a Bayesian marginalization point of view: in the flat basin, each model configuration takes up a substantial volume and contributes a lot to estimating the predictive distribution more precisely. Also, existing flatness-aware methods often use a single solution to represent the whole flat basin, and they ignore that the flat basin has many high-performing models in it. So Bayesian marginalization, by sampling from the flat basins, could potentially give significant improvements over flatness-aware optimization.

Prioritizing flat basins during posterior inference is an additional challenge for Bayesian inference. Even for single point estimation, explicitly biasing toward the flat basins adds substantial computational overhead, like nested loops, calculating gradients twice or min-max problems. This efficiency problem has to be solved before any flatness-aware Bayesian method is practical for deep neural networks.

In this paper we propose an efficient sampling algorithm that explicitly prioritizes flat basins in the energy landscape of deep neural networks. We introduce an auxiliary guiding variable \bm{\theta}_{a} into the Markov chain, which pulls the model parameters \bm{\theta} toward flat basins at each update step (Fig. 1a). \bm{\theta}_{a} is sampled from a smoothed posterior distribution that removes sharp modes based on local entropy (Fig. 1b). \bm{\theta}_{a} can also be seen as obtained by Gaussian convolution, which is a common technique in diffusion models. The joint distribution of \bm{\theta} and \bm{\theta}_{a} in our method is simple, and the computational overhead is similar to Stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD). In theory, we prove that our method is guaranteed to converge faster than some common flatness-aware methods in the strongly convex setting. In experiments, we show that our method finds flat basins efficiently on multiple tasks. Our main contributions are:

- • We propose Entropy-MCMC (EMCMC) to sample from flat basins in the energy landscape of deep neural networks. EMCMC uses an auxiliary guiding variable and a simple joint distribution to steer the model toward flat basins efficiently.

- • We prove that EMCMC converges, and show that it converges faster than several existing flatness-aware methods in the strongly convex setting.

- • We give extensive experimental results that show the advantages of EMCMC for sampling from flat basins. EMCMC is better than all compared baselines on classification, calibration, and out-of-distribution detection, with overhead comparable to SGLD. The code is at https://github.com/lblaoke/EMCMC.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The effectiveness of Bayesian neural networks relies heavily on the quality of the posterior distribution estimate. However, an accurate estimate of the full posterior is extremely difficult to achieve because of its high-dimensional and highly multi-modal nature [1,2]. Moreover, the many modes in the energy landscape typically show varying generalization performance: flat modes often show better accuracy and robustness, whereas sharp modes tend to have high generalization errors [3,4,5]. This connection between the geometry of the energy landscape and generalization has spurred many works in optimization, ranging from theoretical understanding [6,7,8,9] to new optimization algorithms [10,11,12,13].

However, most existing Bayesian methods are not aware of the flatness of the energy landscape during posterior inference [14,15,16,1]. Their inference strategies are usually energy-oriented and cannot distinguish between flat and sharp modes with the same energy values. This limitation can significantly undermine their generalization performance, particularly in practical situations where capturing the full posterior is too costly. We therefore contend that prioritizing the capture of flat modes is essential when performing posterior inference for Bayesian neural networks. This benefits generalization, as justified by previous works [3,4,5]. It can also be rationalized from a Bayesian marginalization perspective: within the flat basin, each model configuration occupies a substantial volume and contributes significantly to a more precise estimate of the predictive distribution [17]. Moreover, existing flatness-aware methods often rely on a single solution to represent the entire flat basin [12,13], ignoring the fact that the flat basin contains many high-performing models. Bayesian marginalization can therefore potentially offer significant improvements over flatness-aware optimization by sampling from the flat basins [18,19].

Prioritizing flat basins during posterior inference poses an additional challenge to Bayesian inference. Even for single point estimation, explicitly biasing toward flat basins introduces substantial computational overhead, in the form of nested loops [12,8], doubled gradient calculations [13,20] or min-max problems [13]. This efficiency problem needs to be addressed before any flatness-aware Bayesian method can become practical for deep neural networks.

In this paper, we propose an efficient sampling algorithm that explicitly prioritizes flat basins in the energy landscape of deep neural networks. Specifically, we introduce an auxiliary guiding variable \bm{\theta}_{a} into the Markov chain to pull the model parameters \bm{\theta} toward flat basins at each update step (Fig. 1a). \bm{\theta}_{a} is sampled from a smoothed posterior distribution which eliminates sharp modes based on local entropy [21] (Fig. 1b). \bm{\theta}_{a} can also be viewed as obtained by Gaussian convolution, a common technique in diffusion models [22,23]. Our method has a simple joint distribution of \bm{\theta} and \bm{\theta}_{a}, and its computational overhead is similar to Stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD) [14]. Theoretically, we prove that our method is guaranteed to converge faster than some common flatness-aware methods [12,8] in the strongly convex setting. Empirically, we show that our method finds flat basins efficiently across multiple tasks. Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

- • We propose Entropy-MCMC (EMCMC) for sampling from flat basins in the energy landscape of deep neural networks. EMCMC uses an auxiliary guiding variable and a simple joint distribution to efficiently steer the model toward flat basins.

- • We prove the convergence of EMCMC and further show that it converges faster than several existing flatness-aware methods in the strongly convex setting.

- • We provide extensive experimental results demonstrating the advantages of EMCMC in sampling from flat basins. EMCMC outperforms all compared baselines on classification, calibration, and out-of-distribution detection with overhead comparable to SGLD. We release the code at https://github.com/lblaoke/EMCMC.
